hints: Look closely at the two six-sided rings, A and D. They look almost identical, so focus on the small difference at carbon 1 on the right side of the ring.
Remember which form of glucose (alpha or beta) links by 1,4 glycosidic bonds to make cellulose, the strong fibre in plant cell walls.
walkthrough:
**Identify each small molecule**

First, let us name what you see. It makes the question much easier.

Molecule A is alpha-glucose, a six-carbon ring sugar. Molecule B is glycerol, a 3-carbon alcohol. Molecule C is adenosine, a nitrogenous base joined to a pentose sugar. Molecule D is beta-glucose, also a six-carbon ring sugar.

**Recall which monomers make structural polymers in plants**

The main structural polymer in plants is cellulose. It strengthens the cell wall.

Cellulose is a polysaccharide made by joining many glucose monomers with 1,4 glycosidic bonds:

**Spot the alpha versus beta difference**

This is the key exam skill. In alpha-glucose (A), the OH on carbon 1 points down. In beta-glucose (D), the OH on carbon 1 points up.

Only beta-glucose can pack together to form straight, strong cellulose microfibrils. So D is the monomer with a structural role.

options.A: This is alpha-glucose. It forms starch in plants and glycogen in animals, both storage polymers, not the structural cellulose.
options.B: This is glycerol. It joins with fatty acids to form triglycerides for energy storage and membranes, not a structural polysaccharide.
options.C: This is the nucleoside adenosine. It is used to build RNA and ATP, not a structural polymer in plant walls.
options.D: This is beta-glucose. Many beta-glucose units join by glycosidic bonds to form cellulose, the structural fibre of plant cell walls.
